opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, not a huge amount, at least not in the precise quantitative outputs. I think of these models as tools for disciplining my intuitions rather than as forecasts I'd bet heavily on.

The basic structure I find fairly compelling: if you have AI systems that can substitute for human labor across a wide range of cognitive tasks, including AI research itself, then you get feedback loops. More AI capability means more effective research labor, which means faster algorithmic progress, which means more capability. Semi-endogenous growth models capture that kind of dynamic reasonably well, and the qualitative conclusion, that you could get a period of very rapid acceleration, seems pretty robust across a lot of parameter choices.

But the specific numbers depend heavily on parameters we just don't know well. How much do returns to research effort diminish as you pick the low-hanging fruit? How substitutable is compute for researcher labor? How bottlenecked are you by experiments, or by physical things like fabs and energy? Small changes in those can move you from "things speed up somewhat" to "extremely fast takeoff," and our empirical estimates mostly come from historical data in regimes that look quite different from a world with automated AI researchers.

There's also the question of whether the models are even carving reality at the right joints. They tend to treat "research labor" as a fairly homogeneous input, when in practice the important thing might be research taste or particular kinds of insight, which could scale very differently.

So my overall stance is: I take the qualitative picture seriously, that software-driven acceleration is plausible and could be fast, and I use the models to sanity-check claims like "this would obviously take decades" or "this would obviously happen in weeks." But I'd put wide error bars on anything more specific, and I try to cross-check against more grounded reasoning, like looking at actual trends in algorithmic efficiency and thinking concretely about what automated researchers would be doing day to day.

r001.rationale: The response says historical estimates come from regimes unlike automated AI research and questions whether the models fit reality, but it does not state that the models were not designed for that regime.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify the size of the growth economics research community as a reason for limited confidence.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not that much — and I want to be careful about what I mean by that, because I think these models are useful in a specific way and misleading in another.

The core thing I take from the growth economics literature is a pretty simple structural point: if you can convert output back into the inputs that produce output — in this case, if AI systems can do the research and engineering that improves AI systems, and if compute can be turned into more compute — then you get feedback loops that can produce extremely fast growth. That basic qualitative conclusion I feel fairly confident in. It doesn't depend on the fine details of any particular model. It's more like, "Here's a mechanism, and once you lift the constraint of human labor being fixed, the mechanism goes wild." I'd put a lot of weight on that.

Where my confidence drops off sharply is when you start asking the models for quantitative answers. How fast is the takeoff? Is it a year from "AIs can do most AI research" to "wildly superhuman systems," or is it a decade? How quickly can you scale up chip fabrication, energy, robotics? The models give you numbers, but those numbers are driven by parameters that we basically have to guess at — returns to research effort, how substitutable AI labor is for human labor, how much the physical world bottlenecks you. Small changes in those parameters swing the output by orders of magnitude. So I treat the models less as prediction machines and more as a way of organizing my intuitions and checking that my story is internally consistent.

There's also a more fundamental worry, which is that these models are calibrated on a world where labor and capital have a particular relationship, and we're asking them to extrapolate into a regime where that relationship breaks. Economists have been pretty good at describing the last 200 years. Whether a Cobb-Douglas production function with some tweaks tells you anything about a world with a billion digital researchers — I'm genuinely unsure. It might, in the same way that simple physics scaling arguments often work better than they should. But it also might not, and I don't think we have great ways to know in advance.

So where I land is: I use the models to say "fast growth is plausible and you shouldn't dismiss it," and to identify which parameters matter most, so I know what to pay attention to as evidence comes in. But if someone told me their model says the economy doubles every six months starting in 2029, I'd think they were fooling themselves about their precision. My own views on timelines and takeoff speeds come more from looking at what current systems can actually do, how fast that's been improving, and thinking directly about the bottlenecks — the models are a sanity check on that, not the source of it.

r001.rationale: It says the models are calibrated on a world with a different labor–capital relationship and questions whether they apply when that relationship breaks, conveying that they were not designed for the advanced-AI regime.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the size of the growth economics research community as a reason for limited confidence.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish confidence in the basic mechanisms from confidence in the quantitative predictions. If AI can substitute for human labor across a very wide range of tasks, including research, there’s a pretty strong reason to expect much faster growth. You can reinvest output in more AI, which can then produce more output and help improve the technology. That’s a potentially very powerful feedback loop.

But I’m much less confident about how fast that actually happens. It depends on what remains bottlenecked by physical infrastructure, how quickly you can build things, and whether improvements in AI translate into useful work as smoothly as the models assume. A fairly simple model can give you a dramatic result, but the simplicity is doing a lot of work.

So I’d treat these models as a way to understand possibilities and identify which assumptions matter, rather than as reliable forecasts of a particular growth rate. I put more confidence in the claim that advanced AI could substantially change the growth regime than in any precise account of the transition.

r001.rationale: The response questions the models’ assumptions and forecasting reliability, but does not say they were not designed for the advanced-AI regime.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the size of the growth economics research community as a reason for limited confidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish confidence in the broad mechanism from confidence in the quantitative predictions. The broad mechanism is that AI could automate the work involved in developing better technology, including better AI. That creates the possibility of a feedback loop, and I think that’s a serious possibility to consider.

But I wouldn’t put much weight on a particular model telling you exactly how fast the economy will grow or how quickly that feedback loop will play out. Those results depend on assumptions about bottlenecks: how much you need physical capital, how quickly you can run experiments, and how easily you can substitute AI for human labour.

So I mostly think of these models as tools for making assumptions explicit and exploring their consequences. They’re useful for seeing why very rapid growth might happen, but they don’t establish that it will happen on a particular timeline.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty in model predictions and their assumptions, but does not say the models were not designed for the advanced AI regime.
